Muscle Building

How many sets and reps you need to build muscle

The old rule of three sets of ten is not wrong, but it hides the variables that actually drive growth: how many hard sets a muscle gets each week, and how close those sets come to failure. Get those two right and the exact rep number matters much less than you were told.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026 · 5 min read

Think in weekly sets, and count them properly

Muscle growth responds to the total amount of hard work a muscle does over a week. Researchers count this as hard sets per muscle per week: sets taken reasonably close to failure, counted for the muscles that do most of the work.

A dose-response meta-analysis by Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (Journal of Sports Sciences, 2017) found that more weekly sets produced more growth, with 10 or more sets per muscle per week outperforming lower volumes. The gains get smaller with each extra set, and past a point, recovery suffers.

Training ageHard sets per muscle per week
Beginner (under 1 year)6-10
Intermediate (1-3 years)10-16
Advanced (3+ years)12-20, varied by muscle

These are starting points. Begin at the low end and add sets only when progress stalls and you are recovering well.

A set counts for a muscle when that muscle is a main mover. A bench press counts for chest and triceps; a row counts for back and biceps. A practical shortcut used by many coaches is to count compound lifts as a full set for the prime mover and a half set for the assisting muscles.

Warm-up sets do not count. Neither do sets you stop with six or more reps still in the tank. If you are not sure whether a set was hard, it probably was not.

Rep ranges: wider than you think

Studies comparing heavy and light loads, including Schoenfeld et al. (Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2017), show that sets of roughly 6 to 30 reps build similar muscle when they are taken close to failure. The rep count changes how the set feels, not whether it works.

RepsBest used forTrade-off
1-5Maximal strength, skill on the big liftsLittle volume per set, more joint stress
6-12Most compound and isolation workThe efficient middle ground
12-20Isolation, machines, joint-friendly workBurning fatigue, harder to judge failure
20-30Small muscles, deload weeks, home trainingLong sets, cardiovascular fatigue limits you

A sensible default is to do your main compound lifts in the 5 to 10 range and your accessories in the 8 to 15 range. Heavy sets still matter if you want to get strong; use the one-rep max calculator to pick loads by percentage.

Proximity to failure and RIR

Effort is what makes a set count. Coaches measure it with reps in reserve (RIR): how many more clean reps you could have done when you stopped.

  • 0 RIR: true failure, the next rep would not go up.
  • 1-2 RIR: the productive zone for most sets.
  • 3-4 RIR: fine for heavy compound lifts and technique work.
  • 5+ RIR: too easy to count as a hard set.

Training to absolute failure on every set adds fatigue faster than it adds growth, especially on squats and deadlifts. Save 0 RIR for the last set of an isolation exercise, where the risk is low.

Beginners nearly always underestimate how many reps they have left. Once in a while, take a safe exercise like a machine curl to true failure to calibrate your sense of what 2 RIR feels like.

How often to train each muscle

Hitting each muscle twice a week tends to produce slightly better growth than once a week at the same total volume (Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger, Sports Medicine, 2016). The main benefit is practical: 14 sets of chest is far better spread over two sessions of 7 than crammed into one.

Splits like the upper lower split and push pull legs naturally train each muscle twice weekly. A full body routine three days a week does the same with fewer exercises per session.

Keep it to roughly 6 to 10 hard sets per muscle in any single session. Beyond that, the quality of later sets drops sharply.

Rest between sets

Short rest periods feel productive but cut the reps you can do on the next set. For compound lifts, rest 2 to 3 minutes. For isolation exercises, 60 to 90 seconds is usually enough.

A good rule: rest until your breathing has settled and you feel able to repeat the previous set's performance. Supersets of non-competing muscles, such as biceps with triceps, save time without much cost.

A sample week

Here is how an intermediate lifter might reach about 12 weekly sets for chest across an upper/lower split:

DayExerciseSets x repsRIR
Upper ABench press3 x 6-82
Upper AIncline dumbbell press3 x 8-121-2
Upper BMachine chest press3 x 10-121
Upper BCable fly3 x 12-150-1

Triceps also get indirect work from every press, which is why they need fewer direct sets than you might expect.

Weekly volume by muscle group

Not every muscle needs the same direct work. Some get plenty of indirect volume from compound lifts; others recover quickly and tolerate more. These ranges are typical starting points for intermediates:

MuscleDirect hard sets/weekNotes
Chest10-16Presses and flies
Back (lats and upper back)12-18Mix vertical pulls and rows
Quads10-16Squats and leg presses are taxing; recover well
Hamstrings and glutes8-14Hinges like Romanian deadlifts plus curls
Shoulders (side and rear delts)8-16Front delts get lots from pressing
Biceps6-12Rows and pull-ups add indirect work
Triceps6-12Every press adds indirect work
Calves and abs6-12Recover quickly; can be trained often

If you are prioritising one muscle, run it near the top of its range and pull a few sets from muscles you are happy to maintain. Maintenance needs surprisingly little: about a third of your normal volume, kept hard, is usually enough for a few months.

Common mistakes

  • Junk volume: piling on sets that stop far short of failure. Five easy sets do less than three hard ones.
  • Too many exercises: six chest movements for two sets each makes it hard to track progress. Two or three exercises done well is plenty.
  • Chasing soreness: soreness reflects novelty more than growth. Rotating exercises constantly to feel sore slows progress.
  • Copying advanced programs: a beginner does not need 20 sets per muscle. Start low and earn the extra volume.
  • Ignoring the log: without writing down weights and reps you cannot tell whether your volume is working.

Adjusting volume when cutting or short on time

In a calorie deficit, recovery drops. Many lifters do best cutting volume by 20 to 30 percent while keeping intensity high. Heavy, hard sets send the signal to keep muscle; extra sets mostly add fatigue you cannot recover from.

If you only have 45 minutes, prioritise in this order: compound lifts for your weakest muscles, then the remaining compounds, then isolation work. Supersets and rest-pause sets can fit more hard sets into the time, at the cost of slightly less weight.

A minimum effective dose for busy weeks is around 4 to 6 hard sets per muscle, spread over two sessions. That will hold most of your progress until life calms down.

How to progress over time

Use a double progression: pick a rep range such as 8 to 12. When you hit 12 on every set at the target RIR, add weight and drop back to 8. This is progressive overload in its simplest form.

If a muscle has stopped growing for six to eight weeks while your diet and sleep are in order, add one or two weekly sets for it. If you feel beaten up, performance is dropping and joints ache, cut volume back by a third for a week, then build up again.

Expect progress to slow as you gain experience. A beginner can add weight almost every week; an advanced lifter may add a rep or two over a month. That is normal, not a sign the program has failed.

None of this works without enough food. If you are eating in a large deficit, more sets will not save you. Check your intake with the calorie calculator and protein calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Is 3 sets of 10 enough to build muscle?

It can be, as long as the sets are hard and the weekly total adds up. Three sets of 10 on two exercises for a muscle, done twice a week, gives 12 weekly sets, which is a solid amount for most people.

Are low reps or high reps better for muscle growth?

Both work for growth when sets are taken close to failure, roughly anywhere from 6 to 30 reps. Low reps are better for building maximal strength, so most programs use a mix.

Can I do too many sets?

Yes. Past about 20 hard sets per muscle per week, most people stop seeing extra growth and start accumulating fatigue and joint pain. If performance is falling, cut volume rather than adding more.

Do I need to train to failure?

No. Stopping one to three reps short of failure gives nearly the same growth with less fatigue. Going to failure occasionally on isolation exercises is fine.
